subject: spaceGalley
pitch:
Category: Prop group.
Subject: spaceship galley kitchen.
Style: Alien (1979) Nostromo.
reasoning:
I'm planning out a single TypeScript module for a static Nostromo-style galley kitchen prop, aiming for a rich model with 180-340 parts and around 700+ lines, using part and extrude geometry builders carefully since I can't test the API directly.

I'm sketching the design: a grimy industrial galley with stainless counters, sink, stove, cabinets, overhead pipes, a bolted mess table, coffee maker, food canisters, vents, control panels with switches and CRT monitors, a fridge locker, hazard-striped wall panels, and fun details like a Jonesy cat food bowl and a Weyland-Yutani logo, all in the beige/cream and brushed steel palette of the original Nostromo set.

Now I'm working out real-world scale -- a roughly 3m-wide, 2.4m-tall, 1.6m-deep module arranged as a back-wall bulkhead with counters, a mess table and benches in front, and a floor deck slab, with everything oriented to face the +Z viewer and positioned starting from a slightly raised floor level.

I'm considering reusing the panelled and metal materials along with rivets from the existing clockwork kit for the bulkhead walls, plus a glow effect from another kit, while building out a Nostromo-style color palette of beige, grey-green, dark charcoal, and amber accents.

For the deck, I'm planning a textured grating/diamond-plate floor with gridlines and noise-based scuffs, plus a hazard-striped border using a diagonal stripe pattern near the front edge. The back bulkhead will use paneled wall boxes, and I'm thinking about adding a recessed window feature too.

Now I'm adding overhead conduits with brackets and valve wheels along the ceiling, plus warm glowing strip light fixtures. I'm also laying out a left-side counter run with a steel base cabinet and countertop slab, working out precise dimensions and positioning relative to the back wall.

Cabinet doors need recessed handle bars, numbered labels, and hazard text, with drawers below. For the sink, I'm building it as a basin recessed into the counter using four slab pieces around a cutout plus interior basin walls and a drain, topped with an industrial gooseneck faucet styled after Nostromo aesthetics. Next to it I'm placing a stovetop with round burners.

Now I'm adding glowing coil rings to the burners, topping them with a lathe-built stock pot with lid and handles plus a saucepan, and giving the fascia labeled control knobs. On the right side I'm planning a tall cold storage unit with frosted steel doors, chunky latches, a glowing digital frost gauge, and a "FOOD STORE 02" label, plus considering an oven built into the base cabinet beneath the hob.

For the oven I'm detailing a door with dark glass window that glows faintly and a handle bar, then moving up to wall cabinets with rounded-rect latch doors and an open shelf for jars and mugs, topped with an extractor hood shaped as a tapered frustum venting up to the ceiling with a fan grille. Between counter and uppers I'm adding a backsplash with a tool rail holding hanging utensils like a ladle, spatula, and whisk. Finally I'm placing a central mess table with bolted pedestal legs and a beige tabletop.

Now I'm working out tabletop items — compartment trays, lathe-turned mugs with torus handles, food packs, a thermos, salt and pepper, a cat bowl labeled "JONESY," and cutlery — plus figuring out bench placement so they don't collide with the counter, nudging the table's z-position to keep clearances workable.

I'm swapping benches for round bolted-down stools instead, three per side, adjusting table and stool positions so everything fits within the deck's depth.

Now I'm laying out the x-axis for this wall: a counter roughly 2.3m wide, then the fridge, then a wall-mounted panel at the far right end with a small glowing CRT-style monitor labeled "GALLEY / MOTHER" at head height.

I'm adding structural details like rib columns with hazard stripes at the side bulkheads, and a header beam with strip lights running along the top instead of a full ceiling so the room stays open from above, with pipes running beneath it. For decals, I'm placing wall labels like a corporate logo, the ship's registration number, "GALLEY," a waste disposal hatch with a flap, and an emergency sign.

Then I'm adding a circular waste chute hatch with a handle, a fridge label, and floor markings. For fun details, I want a tall percolator-style coffee maker with a translucent carafe on the counter, plus the iconic drinking bird toy from the mess hall scene — built from a red glass bulb base, a neck tube, and a head sphere with a beak and tiny top hat on a pivoting stand — placed near the end of the table alongside Jones' cat bowl.

Now I'm planning out the part count, aiming for roughly 200+ pieces built with helper functions like box and cylinder generators, and thinking through how static models can skip joints entirely since everything stays in model space under the root group.

I'm also working out material limits—capping flat colors around 64 by building a palette of about 30 shared colors and relying more on paints and textures, which don't count toward that cap, to add variety like panel details and pot labels without needing sticks, and considering using sweep geometry for pipes or cables where curves are needed.

Now I'm sketching helper functions for building the galley scene: a `box` helper wrapping box geometry with position and color, plane helpers for labels that take a texture and face direction, and cylinder helpers for pots and other rounded shapes, planning to use lathe for pots/mugs/stools, extrude for utensils and trays, and along/ring patterns for rivets and knobs while being careful about orientation.

I'll create a helper function for turned/lathed shapes that takes a profile defined from the axis outward and back, closing the loop along the axis itself since both ends sit on x=0. Now I'm sketching the outline for the pot shape.

I'm checking whether this traces a simple, non-self-intersecting polygon with an inner wall thickness of about 0.015, forming an open-top shell - the sequence of points forms a valid loop without crossing itself.

For the extrude call, I'm working out the right axis orientation so the thickness extends along the correct direction: using x and y basis vectors whose cross product points along +Z works for shapes drawn flat on the XY plane, while for a tray lying flat I need x along x and y along -z so the cross product points up, letting thickness extend vertically.

For sweeps I'll use a Catmull-Rom path with a given radius, round caps, and fewer sides for a chunkier look, and I need to confirm the sweep tool works fine even without an associated bone/joint for static models.

For textures, I'm planning a Weyland-Yutani style logo plate with stylized text, a CRT-style green-on-black status screen with scanlines, and a hazard warning panel design.

I'm also sketching a fridge temperature label with a gauge, and thinking through placing a "JONESY" decal onto the curved surface of the cat bowl — since the bowl is round, I need to use a decal projection onto the bowl part rather than a flat plane to avoid clipping.

For the rest of the environment, I'm planning a control panel with switch labels like "PWR/HEAT/VENT/LIGHTS," a wall stencil reading "GALLEY" with directional arrows and ID codes, and considering a duty roster or menu board for additional detail.

I like the idea of a pinned "CREW ROSTER" sheet listing character names with roles like "DALLAS - CAPT" for flavor, rendered as a cream paper texture with text lines. I'll skip stripe hazard textures in favor of painted stripes, and for food packs I'm thinking small "PROTEIN PASTE" pouch labels plus labeled cans using the lathe shape with applied decals.

For an emergency panel I want a red button with an "EMERGENCY SEAL" sign, and for atmosphere I'll add steam puffs above the pot and coffee maker using double-sided alpha-cut cloud cards attached to frames, keeping them simple white blob shapes with soft gradients.

I'm also planning glow effects for heater coils, indicator lights, the CRT, ceiling panels, and gauges — these need flat-colored or textured materials rather than painted ones, since glow requires a standard mesh material. Now I need to carefully set up coordinates, starting with a deck top height and offset helper for all subsequent placements.

For the back wall, I'm layering a dark backing slab behind paneled cream boxes, positioning four wall panels spaced across the width with small gaps to suggest a frame, keeping them aligned near the bulkhead's front face while overlapping the cabinetry below.

Now I'm thinking about the Nostromo-style color scheme—grey-green industrial tones on the lower walls transitioning to off-white above.

Adding grime near the floor and ceiling vents based on noise, plus a dark horizontal band with an orange stripe accent like the Nostromo corridor look, and confirming the needed helper functions (noise, mix, smoothstep, paint, rgb, resolve) are exported from the builder library.

Now I'm laying out the left counter run: setting cabinet width to 2.2 units centered at x=-0.6, depth 0.62 centered at z=-0.69, with a recessed plinth, a cabinet body rising to F+0.86, and a top slab reaching F+0.9 (so the countertop height is 0.96).

Positioning the plinth, the cabinet box, and the top slab with slightly adjusted depths, then planning a brushed-steel material with edge detailing for the countertop.

Now I'm laying out the countertop pieces, carving out a sink cutout region in the left-center section between roughly x -1.45 and -0.85.

I'm realizing the solid cabinet body box would actually hide the sink basin interior since its top surface sits above where the sink hole should be, so I need to rethink the sink geometry — maybe place the basin floor just below the cabinet's top surface instead of carving a true hole into a solid box.

I'll split the body into left and right pieces plus the lowered sink-bay section, since the closed door hides the lower body anyway. For the basin, I'll set a thin floor and walls flush with the counter top, sized to fit inside the hole opening with a small rim.

Still planning cabinet geometry...

I'm reconsidering the door paint approach—rather than panelled textures causing odd seams on small doors, I want a custom paint that adds a darker beveled edge frame based on normalized UV coordinates, applying it only where the face normal indicates a flat door front.

Now I'm thinking about texel density for the paint atlas: with roughly 40 square meters of total surface area and a 1024-texel sheet, texels would be about 7.4mm, so I'm considering bumping to a 2048 paint size for more crispness given the atlas can go up to 4096.

I'm designing handle hardware as recessed pull bars with small posts and a capsule bar, and laying out the fridge as a tall industrial box with a plinth, split into an upper freezer door and lower door section positioned at the correct depth.

I'm positioning the fridge handle, latch, and a temperature gauge panel with digits, then working out the upper wall cabinet heights relative to the countertop and placing a hood over the stove plus closed cabinets and open shelving around the sink area.

Laying out cabinet widths precisely now: cabinet A on the left with double doors, a hood centered over the stove, an open shelf with jar canisters filling the gap, and a narrow spice rack to the hood's right.

Figuring out the frustumBox orientation for the hood shape — with a vertical y-axis and no explicit up vector, width maps to x and height to z, which clarifies how to position the hood's tapered form above the stove.

Defining the hood wedge outline...

Then I'm adding a chimney duct rising to the ceiling, a fan grille texture on the hood's underside with slat lines and a glow rect, finished in a brushed steel material. I also need a header beam at the wall's top near the ceiling line.

Now I'm placing warm-glowing light strips protruding from the lintel, along with overhead pipe sweeps and brackets running across the top of the scene. I'm also considering side bulkhead panels at the room's edges to partially enclose the space and hide the view from the sides.

Since those side panels might block the camera, I'll replace them with narrow structural ribs or vertical columns at x=±1.8 with hazard-striped bases, plus a vertical pipe on the left. For the mess table, I'm working out its position centered at x=0, z=0.64, sized 1.6 wide, with stool placement on back and front rows checked against clearance from the counter and fridge.

I'm settling on 6 stools split across front and back rows for efficiency, then designing the tabletop as a laminate slab with a steel edge rim underneath, supported by two central cylindrical pedestal legs with base flanges.

For the pedestal detail I'm adding bolt rings, a mounting plate, and an under-stretcher rod, plus a built-in lip for the tabletop. For the stool seat I'm defining a lathe profile with a chamfered edge in ochre vinyl, plus a steel post and rim ring. Then I'm placing a drinking bird toy on the table's right side, building it from a red bulb body, a teal neck tube, and a pivoting leg stand.

For rods and sweeps, I'm setting up helpers that take two points and a radius (or variable radii) plus color/sides options, with a sweep helper that follows a Catmull-Rom path with configurable thickness and cap style.
